Nebraska enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 26-5 team that finished 15-5 in Big Ten play, tied for second in the league during the regular season. Sports-Reference lists the Huskers at 26-5 overall and 15-5 in conference play, while Nebraska’s own Big Ten Tournament preview notes that the Huskers finished the regular season in a three-way tie for second in the league. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/nebraska/men/2026-schedule.html?utm_source=openai))

From a traditional scouting perspective, this is a Fred Hoiberg offense built on spacing, pace into half-court flow, heavy three-point volume, and ball security. Nebraska was averaging 78.6 points per game through 29 games, ranking third in the Big Ten and 18th nationally in made threes at 10.8 per game as of March 2. The Huskers also had 312 made threes through 29 games and had already produced 19 games with at least 10 made threes, including 17 against FIU and Oregon and 15 against Oklahoma and Illinois. Their team assist-to-turnover ratio was 1.91-to-1 on Jan. 12 and rose above 2.00-to-1 later in January, which tells you the offense is not random bombing; it is organized drive-and-kick basketball with extra-pass discipline. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/news/2026/03/2/huskers-look-to-match-school-wins-mark-at-ucla?utm_source=openai))

Specific examples show the structure. Against Oregon on January 13, Nebraska won 90-55 by going 17-of-36 from three, with Pryce Sandfort scoring 28 on 7-of-11 from deep and Braden Frager adding a career-high 23 with seven threes off the bench. Nebraska also recorded 20 assists in that game, a classic Hoiberg marker: spread floor, quick reversal, lift-and-replace shooters, and weak-side kickouts. Against Oklahoma on November 15, Nebraska scored 105 in regulation, hit 15 threes, shot 57.6 percent overall, and got 28 points plus seven assists from Sandfort and 26 points from Rienk Mast, who went 5-of-7 from three. Against Wisconsin on December 10, Nebraska put five players in double figures in a 90-60 win, shot 54 percent, and used a 28-10 closing stretch to the first half after the game was tied 21-19. Those are not isolation games; those are games won through multi-player shot creation and movement. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/news/2026/01/14/no-8-huskers-remain-unbeaten-with-90-55-win-over-oregon?utm_source=openai))

Personnel usage defines the scheme. Sandfort is the primary scoring wing and movement shooter, leading Nebraska at 16.1 points per game while shooting 45 percent from the floor and 37 percent from three. Nebraska’s March 11 tournament preview lists Rienk Mast at 13.6 points, 5.9 rebounds and 2.9 assists, Sam Hoiberg at 9.7 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.4 assists and 2.1 steals, and Braden Frager at 11.7 points and 3.9 rebounds, with Frager named Big Ten Sixth Man of the Year. Jamarques Lawrence functions as another shot-maker/secondary creator; he had a 27-point game at Indiana and a 20-point game at Michigan. That balance is why Nebraska had nine different players with double-figure games by mid-January. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/player/pryce-sandfort?utm_source=openai))

Defensively, Nebraska is more physical and gap-aware than Hoiberg’s reputation suggests. The philosophy is to defend the arc, finish possessions, and force offenses into uncomfortable half-court possessions without donating turnovers. Nebraska held Northwestern, a team averaging a national-best 8.4 turnovers per game, to 11 turnovers in a 77-58 road win on January 17, while also holding the Wildcats to 58 points. In the rematch on February 14, Nebraska held Northwestern to 49 points, its best defensive effort of the season, and outrebounded the Wildcats 40-24. Against Wisconsin on December 10, Nebraska held the Badgers to a season-low 60 points after Wisconsin entered averaging 87.9. Against USC on February 28, Nebraska trailed 37-31 at halftime, then held USC to 39 percent shooting in the second half while dominating the glass 41-25 with 18 offensive rebounds. Even in the loss at Iowa on February 17, Nebraska held Iowa to 33 percent shooting, but the game flipped on Iowa’s plus-10 edges in points off turnovers and offensive rebounds. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/news/2026/01/17/huskers-move-to-18-0-with-win-at-northwestern?utm_source=openai))

Hoiberg’s in-game adjustment history this season is well documented. At Indiana on January 10, Nebraska erased a 16-point second-half deficit to win 83-77, with Lawrence scoring a career-high 27. Against Purdue on February 10, Nebraska trailed by 22 in the second half, then used an 18-2 run to get back in the game and eventually forced overtime before losing 80-77; Mast and Lawrence combined for 12 of Nebraska’s final 15 regulation points. Against Maryland on February 25, Nebraska trailed 48-45 with just over 10 minutes left, then answered with an 18-3 run behind Frager and Mast to win 74-61. Against USC on February 28, the adjustment was rebounding pressure and second-half physicality: Nebraska opened the half on a 12-2 run and took the lead for good 3:02 into the second half. The pattern is clear: Hoiberg is willing to change lineups, increase pace, lean into Frager’s bench scoring, and play through Mast as a facilitator when the first plan stalls. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/news/2026/01/10/huskers-rally-to-top-hoosiers?utm_source=openai))

Late-game execution is one of Nebraska’s biggest differences from prior Hoiberg teams. On December 13, 2025, Nebraska beat No. 13 Illinois 83-80 when Jamarques Lawrence hit the game-winning three with 0.2 seconds left; Sandfort had a career-high 32 and Mast added 17. On January 5, 2026, Nebraska held off Ohio State 72-69 in Columbus, with Braden Frager scoring 15 off the bench in a game ESPN described as Nebraska surviving a late rally. On January 1 against Michigan State, Nebraska trailed 55-52 and held the Spartans to one point over the final 4:30 to win 58-56, with Mast hitting the go-ahead three with 1:50 left. On the other side, Nebraska’s late-game weaknesses also showed up in losses: at Michigan on January 27, the Huskers led 70-65 with 5:52 left but missed eight of their final nine shots and did not score over the last 3:20 in a 75-72 loss. At Iowa on February 17, the offense bottomed out to a season-low 52 points. That gives an opponent a real path: drag the game into the half court and make Nebraska finish through contact late. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/news/2025/12/13/sandfort-posts-career-high-in-buzzer-beater-win-over-no-13-illinois?utm_source=openai))

Key players start with Sandfort, the lead option and biggest matchup problem. He scored 32 against Illinois on December 13, 32 against USC on February 28, 29 against Northwestern on February 14, and 28 against Oregon on January 13. He also set Nebraska’s single-season three-point record at Iowa on February 17, reaching 90 threes. Mast is the all-around frontcourt fulcrum: a midseason All-America selection who was averaging 15.5 points, 6.4 rebounds and 2.9 assists through Nebraska’s 17-0 start; he also posted an 18-point, 12-rebound, 10-assist triple-double against FIU and had 31 against Winthrop. Frager is the microwave reserve who changes games fast: 23 and seven threes vs. Oregon, 21 and eight rebounds vs. Maryland, 20 at Northwestern, and 17 plus eight rebounds at USC. Sam Hoiberg is the connective tissue guard: 9.7 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.4 assists and 2.1 steals per game, plus specific impact lines like 13 points, seven rebounds and five assists at Rutgers and 13 points, seven rebounds, five assists and four steals at Michigan. Lawrence is the clutch combo guard, with the Illinois buzzer-beater, 27 at Indiana, and 20 at Michigan while carrying late-clock creation load. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/player/pryce-sandfort?utm_source=openai))

The notable wins tell you Nebraska’s ceiling. They beat Oklahoma 105-99 after trailing by 16, showing offensive punch and comeback ability. They drilled Wisconsin 90-60, revealing how dangerous they are when their pressure on passing lanes fuels transition threes. They beat No. 13 Illinois 83-80 in Champaign on a last-second shot, proving real road poise. They beat Oregon 90-55 with 17 threes, showing avalanche potential. They beat USC 82-67 on the road by dominating the glass 41-25, showing they can win ugly and physical too. The losses are just as informative. Michigan exposed their short-rotation vulnerability and late-clock stagnation in a 75-72 loss when Mast and Frager were out. Purdue’s 80-77 overtime win exposed issues on the defensive glass, as Purdue won the boards 54-37 and second-chance points 17-6. Iowa’s 57-52 win exposed that if you take away rhythm threes and win turnover/rebounding margins, Nebraska can be ground down. UCLA’s 52-point defensive game against Nebraska on March 4 showed that elite athletic length can squeeze their spacing offense; Nebraska managed only five threes and tied its season low with 52 points. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/news/2025/11/15/huskers-run-past-oklahoma-105-99?utm_source=openai))

As for Hoiberg’s NCAA Tournament history, his record is more substantial than Nebraska alone. At Iowa State, he reached the NCAA Tournament in 2012, 2013, 2014 and 2015. His 2014 team reached the Sweet 16; his 2012 and 2013 teams reached the Round of 32; and his 2015 team lost in the first round. At Nebraska, he led the Huskers to the 2024 NCAA Tournament, where Nebraska lost in the first round, and now has Nebraska back in the 2026 field after the program’s breakthrough regular season. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Hoiberg))

Bottom line: Nebraska is not just a jump-shooting story. It is a veteran, multi-handler, high-assist, high-spacing team with real comeback equity, but its tournament fate will swing on whether Mast can stabilize the interior and whether opponents can force Sandfort and Lawrence into late-clock, one-shot possessions. When Nebraska gets to 80, Hoiberg’s teams usually win; when the game becomes a rebounding-and-turnover grinder like Iowa or Purdue, the Huskers become vulnerable. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/news/2026/01/12/no-8-huskers-look-for-17th-win-tuesday-against-oregon?utm_source=openai))

Nebraska enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with one of the stronger quantitative profiles in the field, even if the team’s underlying shape is a little different from the casual perception of a top-tier Big Ten contender. As of the close of play around Selection Sunday, Nebraska was 26-6 against Division I competition, 15-5 in the Big Ten, with a NET ranking of 14, a KenPom/Pomeroy rank of 14, a BPI rank of 18, and a Bart Torvik T-Rank of 20 on WarrenNolan’s team sheet. Its résumé quality is strong but not purely result-inflated: Nebraska also sat 10th in ESPN Strength of Record and 13th in WAB, while carrying a NET strength of schedule of 34. The non-conference schedule was comparatively soft, however, with a non-conference NET SOS of 306, so a meaningful amount of the team’s profile was built through league play rather than preconference stress testing. The quadrant ledger is excellent: 9-6 in Q1, 6-0 in Q2, 5-0 in Q3, and 6-0 in Q4, with an 11-0 non-conference record overall.

The basic team stats from Nebraska’s official cumulative page show a team that scored 76.0 points per game and allowed 72.6, for a raw scoring margin of +3.4. That modest margin is lower than one might expect for a team ranked in the mid-teens nationally by predictive systems, which is the first clue that Nebraska’s profile is being driven less by gaudy average domination and more by quality wins plus possession-level traits. Nebraska shot 45.6% from the field, 33.5% from three, and 74.9% at the line, while opponents shot 42.7% overall and 33.9% from three. The Huskers attempted 784 threes against 2,035 total field-goal attempts, which yields an approximate 3-point attempt rate of 38.5%. That is a fairly perimeter-oriented shot mix, though not an extreme bombing profile. Their approximate offensive effective field goal percentage was 52.1%, using 928 made field goals and 263 made threes. Their approximate turnover rate was 14.4%, a strong number, and consistent with their 396 turnovers across 35 games, or 11.3 per game. Their approximate free-throw rate was 0.355, and their approximate offensive rebounding rate was just 22.3%, based on 290 offensive rebounds versus 1,009 opponent defensive rebounds. In other words: Nebraska protects the ball well and gets to the line at a healthy clip, but is not especially built around second-chance volume.

That combination helps explain why Nebraska can grade better in predictive systems than the eye test sometimes suggests. This is not an overwhelmingly efficient shot-making team in the way the public often imagines top-15 teams. The 33.5% three-point percentage is solid but not elite, and the offensive rebounding rate is actually fairly modest. What Nebraska does well is avoid empty possessions, maintain offensive structure, and force opponents to earn points against a defense that has been respected by the metrics all year. A February Nebraska game note noted that the Huskers were top-10 nationally in assist-to-turnover ratio and had steadily improved in KenPom defensive efficiency as the season progressed. External KenPom aggregation coverage from late February characterized Nebraska as a defense-first team, listing it roughly as No. 8 nationally on defense and No. 41 on offense at that snapshot. That framing fits the broad consensus of the data much better than the conventional storyline that Nebraska is simply an explosive offensive breakout team.

The divergence between résumé and perception is even more interesting when you compare raw and adjusted viewpoints. Nebraska’s raw per-game margin of +3.4 is not what you expect from a high-end protected seed candidate. But the predictive systems continued to buy the Huskers because they had top-20 caliber underlying strength, especially on the defensive end, and because they accumulated a substantial number of high-value wins without taking bad losses. Nebraska beat Oklahoma 105-99 on a neutral floor, New Mexico 84-72 at a neutral site, Wisconsin 90-60, Indiana 83-77 on the road, Ohio State 72-69 on the road, Washington 76-66, Rutgers 80-68 on the road, USC 82-67 on the road, Iowa 84-75, and Maryland 74-61, among others. They also logged losses that were mostly respectable: at Michigan 72-75, at Iowa 52-57, at UCLA 52-72, home against Illinois 69-78, home against Purdue 77-80, and a neutral-site loss to Purdue 58-74 in the Big Ten tournament. That pattern matters: Nebraska’s downside games came against credible opponents, and its ceiling results were real.

Recent form was good, though not perfect. The official stats page listed Nebraska on a four-game winning streak at the time of the cumulative update, while WarrenNolan’s team sheet confirms a late-season run including wins over Penn State on February 21, Maryland on February 25, USC on February 28, and Iowa on March 8 before the neutral-court loss to Purdue on March 13. So the trend line entering the bracket was positive in results terms, with Nebraska stabilizing after road losses to Iowa and UCLA. I could not locate a fully accessible public source with exact adjusted offensive and defensive efficiency splits specifically for the last 10 games, but the available evidence points to a team whose defense remained the anchor while the offense oscillated based on perimeter variance and whistle generation. The win at USC, the solid close to league play, and the absence of any late collapse all support the view of Nebraska as a team arriving in reasonably good shape.

On personnel, Brice Williams was the offensive headliner at 20.4 points per game, with Juwan Gary at 14.6 and Connor Essegian at 10.7. The roster distribution reinforces the statistical identity: enough creators to avoid stagnation, enough spacing to create free-throw pressure, and enough veteran ball security to keep the floor high. But the numbers do not portray Nebraska as a dominant glass team or a pure shotmaking machine. Instead, this is a disciplined, relatively low-mistake, defense-tilted team with a tournament-worthy résumé and predictive support to match.

Bottom line: Nebraska’s 2026 profile is that of a legitimate second-weekend threat because the Huskers are stronger on defense and possession management than public perception may credit. The eye test may sometimes see a team that wins ugly, lacks overwhelming rebounding pop, and can look ordinary from three. The metrics see something more stable: a top-20 national team with a top-15 résumé, a strong Q1 portfolio, low turnover offense, respectable shot profile, and enough defensive quality to travel in March.
matchup-analyst:
Nebraska enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a Fred Hoiberg team that wins with spacing, ball security, veteran frontcourt skill, and secondary playmaking from multiple positions. Through March 2, Nebraska was 25-4, averaging 78.6 points per game while allowing 65.4, shooting .468 from the field, .357 from three, posting 18.3 assists per game against only 9.6 turnovers, and forcing 7.3 steals per game. Their +3.6 turnover margin and 1.9 assist/turnover ratio are central to how they control games. ([uclabruins.com](https://uclabruins.com/documents/download/2026/3/2/Nebraska_Notes_March03.pdf))

Style of play: Nebraska is most dangerous when its frontcourt can function as passers and floor-spacers around Pryce Sandfort and Rienk Mast. Sandfort is the primary matchup problem: he was averaging 19.4 points per game on Sports-Reference, and Nebraska’s March 2 notes highlight multiple 30-point games, including 32 at USC. Mast was averaging 13.7 points, 6.1 rebounds, and 3.1 assists, giving Nebraska a 6-10 hub who can score inside, pop, and pass. Sam Hoiberg adds connective tissue rather than pure shot creation; he carried a 5.04 assist-to-turnover ratio, one of the best national marks listed in Nebraska’s notes. That profile says Nebraska prefers read-and-react team offense over stagnant pounding. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/nebraska/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

The tactics that disrupt this offense are the ones that deny comfortable reversals and force them into late-clock individual creation. The clearest evidence is the February 1 home loss to Illinois. Nebraska still got 8 fast-break points and 24 bench points, but Illinois held them to 69 points, won the paint 28-18, and Nebraska scored only 30 second-half points after leading 39-33 at halftime. That is a game where Nebraska’s normal balanced attack stalled once the game became more physical and interior-oriented. Purdue also disrupted them on February 10 by building a 22-point lead; Nebraska came back but still lost 80-77 in overtime while giving up 17 second-chance points and trailing in time-with-lead 41:47 to 1:25. Those games suggest the pressure points are: shrink the paint, switch enough to take away pick-and-pop rhythm, and make Nebraska win through contested isolation jumpers rather than scripted touch-sharing. ([storage.googleapis.com](https://storage.googleapis.com/huskers-com-prod/2026/02/01/ddPuzPRKlU3Ss7Bf38cCVHf7NLtHO0nKH1p5iKfW.pdf))

Press vulnerability: the season-long numbers actually argue Nebraska is hard to rattle with conventional pressure. Their 9.6 turnovers per game and 1.9 assist/turnover ratio are elite markers of press resistance, and by March 2 they had forced 380 opponent turnovers while committing only 277 themselves. Sam Hoiberg is a major reason; his 5.04 A/TO ratio is exactly the profile you do not want to press casually. So if you press Nebraska, it cannot be for steal volume alone; it has to be a selective, after-make or sideline-trap press designed to burn clock and force them to start offense at 20 seconds or less. The evidence against heavy gambling is in games Nebraska handled cleanly: at Illinois on December 13 they had only 8 turnovers in an 83-80 road win, and against Washington their game notes showed Nebraska at 9.1 turnovers per game entering that matchup. ([uclabruins.com](https://uclabruins.com/documents/download/2026/3/2/Nebraska_Notes_March03.pdf))

Zone vulnerability: there is less direct public play-type evidence available than for press handling, but the named-game evidence still points to a specific weak point. Illinois beat Nebraska on February 1 while Nebraska managed only 18 paint points and shot profile leaned jump-shot heavy; that is the kind of stat line usually produced when a defense successfully walls the lane and forces perimeter decision-making. By contrast, when Nebraska gets the ball moving freely against more open man or scrambling coverages, the ceiling is obvious: 90 against Wisconsin, 90 against Oregon, 87 against Penn State, and 82 at USC. The tactical takeaway is that compact zone principles with sharp closeouts matter more than pure zone volume: tag Mast on short-roll catches, top-lock Sandfort on the weak side, and live with secondary above-the-break threes from lower-usage pieces. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/sports/mens-basketball/schedule/season/2025-26))

Preferred pace: Nebraska is not a pure track-meet team, but it is clearly more comfortable when it can score before the defense is set and then play from ahead. The Illinois road win on December 13 featured 7-4 Nebraska edge in fast-break points and an 83-point output. Against USC on February 28, Nebraska flipped a 36-31 halftime deficit into an 82-67 win by dominating the glass 41-25 with 18 offensive rebounds and opening the second half on a 12-2 run. They can run, but more accurately they thrive in “advantage pace” — early offense created from rebounds, steals, and quick hits before full help is loaded. ([storage.googleapis.com](https://storage.googleapis.com/huskers-com-prod/2025/12/13/7SgGNTbSgz6ufV0JppvW8ay8WYPfzwiHRz321cDB.pdf))

To force the opposite, you have to make Nebraska play deep into the clock, every trip. Do not give them live-ball turnovers, because their season edge in turnover margin is too strong. Send two guards back in transition, prioritize floor balance over offensive rebounding, and on offense use long, physical possessions that attack Mast and Sandfort in screening actions. The goal is not just to slow tempo; it is to remove their possession-quality edge. Nebraska is 17-1 when holding opponents under 1.00 points per possession, so if you allow them to dictate efficiency terms, the game is usually over. ([uclabruins.com](https://uclabruins.com/documents/download/2026/3/2/Nebraska_Notes_March03.pdf))

Size/athleticism mismatches by position: at point guard, Sam Hoiberg is only 6-0, 180, so explosive downhill guards can try to shoot over him or force switches onto him, even though his steal/rebound production makes him tougher than his size suggests. At the wing, Connor Essegian is 6-4/205 and more of a spacing piece than an elite stopper; that can be attacked with bigger slashers. Jamarques Lawrence at 6-3 gives them another smallish guard line. The real bulk is up front: Pryce Sandfort is 6-7/210, Braden Frager 6-7/215, Berke Buyuktuncel 6-10/244, and Mast 6-10/250. That means small-ball opponents can create speed mismatches at the 4/5, but traditional teams may struggle with Nebraska’s size and skill. Frager’s production matters here: Nebraska’s notes list him at 12.7 points per game, and he had 17 points and 8 rebounds at USC. If your 3-man is undersized, Nebraska can punish it with Frager/Sandfort screening and crashing. Conversely, if you have an NBA-caliber quick 4, you can pull Mast or Buyuktuncel into space. ([huskers.com](https://huskers.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/season/2025-26))

Isolation vs. team offense tendencies: publicly accessible team sheets here do not provide a verified Synergy isolation percentage, so I cannot honestly fabricate an isolation-rate number. What the available numbers do show is strong team-offense lean: 18.3 assists per game, 1.9 A/TO ratio, and multiple frontcourt passers. Nebraska’s best offensive games also feature distributed creation rather than one-man ball: in the 90-60 Wisconsin win, Mast had 17, Hoiberg 12, Lawrence 5 assists, Frager 15, and Buyuktuncel 14; at USC, Sandfort had 32 but Frager added 17 and Nebraska won the glass 41-25. The inference is that Nebraska prefers assisted flow and matchup hunting through actions, not sustained pure isolation. That is an inference from assist and box-score distribution, not a direct Synergy isolation percentage. ([uclabruins.com](https://uclabruins.com/documents/download/2026/3/2/Nebraska_Notes_March03.pdf))

Transition offense/defense frequency: exact possession-frequency percentages were not available in the public sources I could verify, but Nebraska’s game evidence shows transition is a meaningful additive, not the entire offense. They had 7 fast-break points at Illinois in the road win, 8 in the home loss to Illinois, only 4 in the Purdue loss, and 7 against USC Upstate. That pattern suggests they can win without huge transition volume, but their best version gets some easy offense while keeping opponents from doing the same. Defensively, their 7.3 steals per game and +3.6 turnover margin are the clearest transition-creation indicators. ([storage.googleapis.com](https://storage.googleapis.com/huskers-com-prod/2025/12/13/7SgGNTbSgz6ufV0JppvW8ay8WYPfzwiHRz321cDB.pdf))

Coaching adaptability: yes, Hoiberg’s staff has concrete evidence of in-game adjustment. Against USC on February 28, Nebraska trailed 36-31 at the half, then opened the second half on a 12-2 run, took control, and held USC to 31 second-half points while winning the glass 41-25. Nebraska’s own notes also mention four double-figure comebacks in 2024-25 and a pattern of resilience under this staff, but the strongest 2025-26 example is that USC reversal. The Purdue game also shows bench and schematic poise: Nebraska erased a 22-point deficit and forced overtime, even if it lost. That is real adjustment evidence, though “mid-series” is less applicable in college than in playoff formats; the better framing is strong halftime and late-game adaptability. ([usctrojans.com](https://usctrojans.com/news/2026/2/28/usc-mens-basketball-falters-against-no-12-nebraska?utm_source=openai))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Nebraska you must 1) keep them out of advantage offense by eliminating live-ball turnovers and sending two guards back; 2) crowd the lane with zone principles or gap-help man so Mast’s interior passing becomes kick-out volume instead of rim volume; 3) force Hoiberg, Lawrence, and Essegian to finish over length rather than letting Sandfort/Mast initiate cleanly; 4) attack Nebraska’s small guards with physical screening to generate switches; 5) punish them on the offensive glass, because Purdue’s 17 second-chance points and Illinois’ 19 second-chance points in Champaign were proof that Nebraska can be moved backward physically; and 6) make the game ugly and half-court heavy, because Nebraska’s best statistical edges are ball security, assisted offense, and transition creation. If you let Nebraska play clean, connected basketball, the numbers say they usually win.
